summary: Lists requirements for a quality of service solution for Mobile IP. Mobile IP routes packets to a moving device, but the packets also need proper forwarding treatment along the new path so QoS-sensitive services work. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone moves, the internet can keep finding it, but video calls also need the fast lane to follow. This memo lists what that would need.

questions: quality of service for mobile ip
subtitle: What Mobile IP needs from quality-of-service mechanisms to work well.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP allows devices to keep communicating when they move, but as the device's path through the network changes, the quality-of-service (fast lanes, priority handling) rules that were set up for the old path no longer apply. New paths may go through different networks with different QoS systems, and packets can get stuck without proper treatment.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists requirements for QoS systems to work with Mobile IP, including minimizing interruption when a device hands over, limiting QoS re-establishment to affected path segments, releasing old QoS rules, handling heterogeneous QoS paradigms, and protecting against spoofed handover attacks.
tldr.outcome: The document provided guidance for designing or extending QoS mechanisms to support mobile nodes, though it does not define solutions. It was published as Informational to shape future QoS and Mobile IP protocol development.

facts.label: Key problem
facts.value: Care-of address change breaks QoS flow identification

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: IPv4 and IPv6 Mobile IP (not specific to one version)

today: RFC 3583 is Informational and provided guidance for the development of Mobile IP QoS solutions. Various QoS and mobility mechanisms have been deployed since (RSVP-TE for MPLS traffic engineering, DiffServ with tunnel marking, MIPv6 with local mobility anchors), though comprehensive QoS-aware Mobile IP solutions remain an area of ongoing research and deployment trade-offs.

sections.title: The Mobile IP and QoS Problem
sections.content:
Mobile IP enables a device to change its attachment point to the Internet (such as moving from one cellular network to another, or from cellular to WiFi) while maintaining ongoing communication sessions. However, Mobile IP only solves the routing problem: it ensures packets reach the moving device's current location. It does not automatically ensure that quality-of-service (QoS) treatment—packet prioritization, bandwidth reservation, latency bounds—follows the device along the new path.

When a device undergoes handover to a new access router, the path that packets traverse changes. This may affect only a small segment near the mobile node (local handover) or change the entire path from end to end (wide-area handover). Additionally, the device may be assigned a new care-of address (the temporary address used for routing while away from home), which breaks existing QoS bindings that use IP addresses as keys. Meanwhile, the new access network might employ a completely different QoS paradigm (for example, switching from a Differentiated Services network to an Integrated Services network), requiring different signaling and setup mechanisms.

The RFC addresses these challenges by identifying the requirements that QoS mechanisms must satisfy to work reliably with Mobile IP, preparing the ground for future protocol development and design choices.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IP keeps your packets finding you as you move, but it does not keep your priority lane. If your video call needs the fast lane, we need to set that up again on the new path. This memo lists what needs to happen.

sections.title: Performance Requirements
sections.content:
The first critical requirement is to minimize QoS interruption at handover time. Before the new access router learns about the mobile node's QoS needs, packets may arrive without the correct forwarding treatment and receive only default (best-effort) handling. The RFC defines a metric for this: the number of packets served with default QoS should be minimized. When a care-of address changes after handover (which is common in IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration), existing RSVP signaling (one popular QoS mechanism) requires one round-trip time before the new path can be set up, meaning many packets experience default treatment during this window. This latency is unacceptable during an active session, though it might be acceptable at session initiation.

The second requirement is to localize QoS (re)establishment to the affected portions of the path. In many cases, only a small segment of the path near the mobile node changes; the rest remains stable. Ideally, the QoS mechanism should limit signaling and reservation changes to just the affected segment, conserving network resources and time. However, when the care-of address changes, some nodes along the unchanged path might rely on IP addresses as QoS flow identifiers, requiring updates even where the physical path is unaltered. Moreover, if handover causes an end-to-end path change (such as moving between administrative domains), QoS must be established across the entire new path.

The third requirement is to release QoS state along the old path after handover. Resources reserved or rules installed on the old path are no longer needed and should be freed. During handover, the mobile node may lose link-layer connectivity to the old access router, preventing it from sending explicit teardown messages, so the QoS mechanism must support either explicit release (the mobile node or new network sends a teardown) or timer-based cleanup (reservations expire after a timeout).
sections.plainLanguage: Three hard problems: packets get bad treatment while you move, we should only fix the changed parts of the path, and old rules should be cleaned up. The RFC says all three must be solved.

sections.title: Interoperability and Heterogeneity
sections.content:
A QoS solution for Mobile IP must interoperate with other mobility protocols. Several complementary technologies—fast handover protocols (to reduce handover latency), localized mobility management (to support hierarchical mobility without involving the home network), and context transfer (to move protocol state between routers)—can optimize Mobile IP operation. A good QoS solution should take advantage of these mechanisms when available, but it must also work correctly even if they are not deployed.

The second interoperability challenge is heterogeneous QoS paradigms. Different network domains use different QoS approaches. IntServ (Integrated Services) relies on explicit end-to-end RSVP signaling to reserve bandwidth for specific flows. DiffServ (Differentiated Services) uses edge routers to mark packets and core routers to provide corresponding classes of service without per-flow state. When a mobile node hands over from a DiffServ-based access network to an IntServ-based network, the QoS mechanism must adapt: it must stop relying on DiffServ packet marking and instead trigger RSVP reservations suitable for IntServ. The RFC emphasizes that a single QoS mechanism should handle this heterogeneity seamlessly, or at least provide mechanisms for detection and adaptation.

Supporting multiple potential paths is another interoperability need. After handover, a mobile node's packets may traverse different routes: a direct route-optimized path to the correspondent node, a triangle route via the home agent, a temporary tunnel between old and new access routers, or a reverse tunnel for security. A comprehensive QoS solution should address QoS setup along all relevant paths, though policy, privacy, and mobility considerations may dictate which paths are actually used.
sections.plainLanguage: QoS with Mobile IP must work with other mobility helpers, handle networks that use different QoS styles, and support packets taking different paths. One size does not fit all, so flexibility matters.

sections.title: Additional Requirements and Security
sections.content:
The RFC identifies a miscellaneous requirement for QoS information to be meaningful to wireless link layers. Mobile devices often connect via wireless, where link-layer characteristics (error correction, power, modulation) interact with application needs. A QoS mechanism should provide information (such as acceptable packet loss rates) that helps both IP-layer applications make service choices and wireless link managers select appropriate modulation and error correction. This allows an application requiring low loss to request a QoS service with that property, and the wireless link can then apply stronger error correction if needed.

Standard requirements apply: the solution should be scalable, secure, conserve wireless bandwidth, impose low overhead on mobile terminals, provide hooks for authorization and accounting, and remain robust if Mobile IP-specific QoS components fail. While precise quantitative targets are not set, these criteria provide a framework for evaluating candidates.

Security is critical. A malicious node might spoof QoS handover signaling to trick the network into believing a mobile node has moved when it has not, causing the network to tear down valid QoS or install incorrect rules. This could disrupt ongoing sessions or waste network resources. The QoS mechanism must allow intermediate nodes to verify that QoS signaling is authentic and initiated by authorized parties, not by attackers.
sections.plainLanguage: QoS information should help wireless links decide how strong to make error correction. The whole system should be scalable, not waste power, and not trust handover messages from attackers.

sections.title: Approach and Next Steps
sections.content:
The RFC identifies an approach to solving the Mobile IP QoS problem in four steps: (1) list requirements (which the RFC addresses), (2) evaluate existing QoS solutions against those requirements, (3) decide whether to extend current solutions or define new ones, and (4) implement the chosen approach. The RFC focuses exclusively on step 1 and provides context for steps 2 and 3 by highlighting shortcomings of well-known proposals (notably, RSVP) when used directly with Mobile IP.

The document emphasizes that the requirements apply to both IPv4 and IPv6 Mobile IP. The same mechanisms might be used for both versions, or separate solutions might be designed for each. The RFC assumes that target access router selection is handled by other protocols (such as Seamoby Fast Handover or Candidate Access Router Discovery), so QoS-based handover decisions are out of scope.

By documenting these requirements, the RFC provides a specification and evaluation framework for future working groups to use when designing or selecting QoS solutions for mobile nodes. It serves as a checklist: does the proposed solution minimize handover QoS interruption? Does it localize signaling to affected segments? Does it support heterogeneous QoS paradigms? Answers to these questions help assess whether a solution is suitable for practical Mobile IP deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo lists what any QoS solution for Mobile IP must do. Future standards can use this checklist to decide whether their design works for moving devices.
